questions.prompt: What is the primary definition of Dependency Injection in iOS architecture?

options.text: Supplying needed helper objects from the outside rather than creating them internally
options.explanation: Dependency Injection means passing collaborator objects into a class instead of letting the class construct them.

options.text: Injecting binary machine code directly into device memory during runtime
options.explanation: This describes dynamic memory exploitation, not an architectural pattern.

options.text: Storing all application model properties inside a global dictionary
options.explanation: Global dictionaries represent global state or service locators, not clean dependency injection.

options.text: Automatically downloading external third-party libraries over the network
options.explanation: Downloading libraries is handled by package managers like Swift Package Manager.

questions.prompt: Which dependency injection technique is considered the standard preference in Swift?

options.text: Method injection on every single private function
options.explanation: Method injection is useful only when a dependency varies per function call.

options.text: Initializer injection using constructor arguments
options.explanation: Initializer injection guarantees properties are set before use and enables immutable let constants.

options.text: Property injection using implicitly unwrapped optionals
options.explanation: Property injection leaves objects vulnerable to nil reference crashes before assignment.

options.text: Global singleton access through static variables
options.explanation: Singletons create tight coupling and are the opposite of dependency injection.

questions.prompt: How does dependency injection improve unit testability?

options.text: It forces tests to run directly on physical iOS hardware
options.explanation: Unit tests run faster in headless simulator or host environments.

options.text: It eliminates the need to compile test targets
options.explanation: Test targets still compile normally.

options.text: It enables tests to pass mock objects instead of real services
options.explanation: Tests can substitute network or storage dependencies with fast, deterministic test doubles.

options.text: It turns all class reference types into value types
options.explanation: Dependency injection does not change Swift memory semantics.

questions.prompt: What design principle is closely related to Dependency Injection?

options.text: Copy on Write
options.explanation: Copy on Write is an optimization mechanism for value types in Swift.

options.text: Manual Memory Management
options.explanation: Swift uses Automatic Reference Counting (ARC) rather than manual memory management.

options.text: Premature Optimization
options.explanation: Premature optimization is a programming pitfall, not an architectural pattern.

options.text: Inversion of Control
options.explanation: Dependency Injection is a concrete implementation of Inversion of Control.

questions.prompt: When decoupling a consumer from a concrete service, what should sit between them?

options.text: A Swift protocol defining the required operations
options.explanation: Protocols create an abstract contract boundary between consumers and concrete implementations.

options.text: A global notification center observer
options.explanation: NotificationCenter introduces loose messaging but obscures API contracts.

options.text: A C pointer reference
options.explanation: Swift protocols provide type-safe abstractions without raw pointers.

options.text: A persistent SQLite database table
options.explanation: Databases store data, not architectural abstractions.

questions.prompt: Why is declaring injected dependencies as let constants advantageous in Swift?

options.text: It permits the dependency to be reassigned during runtime
options.explanation: let constants cannot be reassigned after initialization.

options.text: It guarantees immutability and thread safety for the reference
options.explanation: let ensures the collaborator reference cannot be unexpectedly mutated or set to nil.

options.text: It causes the class to be automatically deallocated
options.explanation: let does not alter ARC deallocation behavior.

options.text: It bypasses Swift concurrency checks entirely
options.explanation: Swift concurrency applies equally to let and var properties.

questions.prompt: How does a default argument in an initializer support dependency injection?

options.text: It forbids callers from providing custom mocks
options.explanation: Callers can still provide custom arguments to override the default.

options.text: It stores dependencies inside persistent keychain storage
options.explanation: Default arguments are evaluated at the call site, not stored in the keychain.

options.text: It provides convenient production instantiation while retaining test mockability
options.explanation: Production code can call init() with the default service, while tests can pass a mock.

options.text: It prevents the class from compiling in debug builds
options.explanation: Default arguments compile cleanly in both debug and release builds.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism provides built-in dependency injection across a SwiftUI view tree?

options.text: @StateObject bindings
options.explanation: @StateObject manages lifecycle for an ObservableObject, not tree-wide DI.

options.text: Core Data managed object contexts
options.explanation: Core Data is a persistence framework, though managed contexts can be placed in the environment.

options.text: Static singleton properties on AppDelegate
options.explanation: AppDelegate singletons are global and not native SwiftUI tree injection.

options.text: SwiftUI EnvironmentValues using the @Environment property wrapper
options.explanation: @Environment allows parent views to propagate values and services down to all descendants.

questions.prompt: What is property injection, and when is it commonly encountered in iOS?

options.text: Assigning dependencies to mutable variables after instantiation, common in UIKit storyboards
options.explanation: When storyboards create view controllers, dependencies must often be set on properties afterwards.

options.text: Passing parameters to global C functions during app launch
options.explanation: Passing arguments to functions is parameter passing, not property injection.

options.text: Declaring computed properties that instantiate new objects every access
options.explanation: Creating new instances in computed properties is not dependency injection.

options.text: Writing values directly to UserDefaults
options.explanation: UserDefaults is persistence, not dependency injection.

questions.prompt: Why is the Service Locator pattern often criticized compared to initializer injection?

options.text: It requires writing extra protocols for every model struct
options.explanation: Service locators do not require extra protocols on models.

options.text: It hides class dependencies and defers missing dependency errors to runtime crashes
options.explanation: With a service locator, you cannot tell what dependencies a class needs by inspecting its initializer.

options.text: It makes apps run too quickly for profiling tools
options.explanation: Service locators do not artificially speed up code.

options.text: It prevents classes from being compiled with Swift 6
options.explanation: Service locators compile in Swift 6, but they represent an architectural anti-pattern.

questions.prompt: What problem occurs when business logic calls URLSession.shared directly?

options.text: URLSession.shared deletes user authentication tokens automatically
options.explanation: URLSession.shared does not delete tokens.

options.text: The operating system refuses to execute HTTP requests
options.explanation: URLSession.shared executes requests normally in production.

options.text: Unit tests cannot run without hitting real network endpoints
options.explanation: Hardcoded singletons prevent tests from substituting network responses with local mocks.

options.text: Swift compiler disables optimization passes
options.explanation: Singletons have no effect on compiler optimization passes.

questions.prompt: When might using a third-party dependency injection framework become a disadvantage?

options.text: When the framework is written in pure Swift
options.explanation: Being written in Swift is generally an advantage.

options.text: When building an app with SwiftUI views
options.explanation: Frameworks can work with SwiftUI, but may add unnecessary overhead.

options.text: When the project requires unit tests
options.explanation: Unit testing is supported by DI frameworks.

options.text: When it adds runtime reflection magic and hides compile-time type verification
options.explanation: Complex containers can obscure missing dependencies until runtime and add build complexity.

questions.prompt: What is the Composition Root in an iOS application architecture?

options.text: The unified location where modules and dependencies are assembled together
options.explanation: The composition root (such as App launch or main coordinators) instantiates concrete dependencies and wires them up.

options.text: The root folder containing the Xcode project file
options.explanation: Composition root is a software architecture concept, not a filesystem directory.

options.text: The top-most superclass in an Objective-C class hierarchy
options.explanation: NSObject is the root class, not the composition root.

options.text: A database schema migration file
options.explanation: Composition root has nothing to do with database migrations.

questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview
questions.prompt: How does dependency injection interact with Swift 6 strict concurrency checks?

options.text: Injected services are exempt from Sendable verification
options.explanation: All types passed across isolation boundaries must comply with Sendable in Swift 6.

options.text: Injected protocols passed across concurrency domains must conform to Sendable
options.explanation: To prevent data races when dependencies are accessed across actors or threads, protocols must be Sendable.

options.text: Dependencies can only be passed using nonisolated unsafe pointers
options.explanation: Unsafe pointers violate Swift 6 concurrency safety goals.

options.text: Swift 6 forbids initializer injection entirely
options.explanation: Initializer injection is completely compatible and encouraged in Swift 6.

questions.prompt: Which combination represents the cleanest idiomatic dependency injection in Swift?

options.text: Global service locator with force unwrapped optional variables
options.explanation: Global locators and force unwrapping are fragile and obscure dependencies.

options.text: Property injection using public variables mutated from anywhere
options.explanation: Public mutable properties allow unintended state modifications.

options.text: Protocol abstractions with constructor initializer injection
options.explanation: Protocols provide abstraction while initializer injection guarantees compile-time immutability and testability.

options.text: Concrete singleton classes referencing shared instances directly
options.explanation: Hardcoded singletons tightly couple code and destroy testability.

questions.prompt: Explain what Dependency Injection means and why developers use it in iOS apps. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Defines dependency injection as passing collaborator objects from the outside rather than creating them internally
Identifies key benefits such as isolated unit testing, loose coupling, or implementation swapping

questions.prompt: Compare initializer injection with property injection. Why is initializer injection usually preferred in Swift? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that initializer injection passes dependencies at creation time, enabling let constants and preventing invalid state
Contrasts with property injection which requires mutable variables and risks uninitialized nil errors

questions.prompt: Why is the Service Locator pattern considered an anti-pattern when compared to explicit initializer injection? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that service locators hide class dependencies from initializers and compiler type checking
Notes that missing dependencies fail at runtime instead of compile time and complicate unit testing
